chunks: I would rather spend a night in wakefulness on the thorns of the sa'dan plant, or be dragged in chains as a prisoner, than meet Allah and His Messenger on the Day of Resurrection as an oppressor to any of the servants, or a usurper of anything out of worldly wealth.
And how can I oppress anyone for a life that hastens towards destruction in its return, and remains long in the earth in its settlement?!

key_terms.السَّعْدَانِ: A plant with sharp prickles, used here to symbolize painful physical discomfort
key_terms.قُفُولُهَا: Its return or journey (referring to the brevity of life)

ai.seo_question: Why does Imam Ali prefer hardship over oppression?
ai.summary: In this famous hadith from Nahj al-Balagha, Imam Ali (AS) illustrates the profound weight of *Dhulm* (injustice) by contrasting it with the physical suffering of sleeplessness or shackles, prioritizing spiritual integrity over material accumulation. He rhetorically questions the logic of oppressing beings whose return to dust is inevitable, highlighting the transient nature of worldly possessions (*al-hutam*) versus the eternal accountability before God. This passage is central to Shia political ethics, emphasizing that leadership requires a higher tolerance for personal hardship than for the burden of wronging the people.
